name: Ismarus

claims.text: The Odyssey places Ismarus on the Thracian coast, home of the Cicones.
The Cicones are attested as a real Thracian people and Trojan allies in the Iliad.
This stop reflects a geographically plausible route rather than fantastical geography, unlike the stops that follow.

summary: Odysseus's first stop after leaving Troy — a real Thracian coast, sacked and immediately regretted.
myth: Odysseus raids the city of the Cicones, allies of Troy, for plunder. His men linger to feast instead of leaving, and the Cicones return with reinforcements and kill six men from each ship before the fleet escapes. It is the first sign that the journey home will go wrong.
historicalBackground: Unlike almost everywhere else in the poem, Ismarus sits on a real, identifiable stretch of coast that a fleet leaving Troy for Greece would plausibly pass — the Cicones are a real Thracian people named elsewhere in the Iliad as Trojan allies.

name: Land of the Lotus-Eaters

claims.text: The Odyssey describes a plant that erases the desire to return home.
Homer does not provide enough geographical information to identify the land securely.
The island of Djerba is the location of the Lotus-Eaters.

summary: A land where the fruit itself is the danger — eat it, and the desire to ever go home disappears.
myth: A storm off Cape Malea drives the fleet nine days south. Scouts sent ashore eat the lotus plant and lose all wish to return — Odysseus has to drag them back to the ships in tears and tie them under the rowing benches.
historicalBackground: Homer gives no coordinates; "nine days before the north wind" is a narrative device, not a distance. Djerba is the most commonly cited traditional identification, on the strength of a local lotus-like plant and a long-standing (though modern) tourist tradition — not an ancient one.

name: Island of the Cyclopes

claims.text: Odysseus blinds Polyphemus and escapes by giving a false name, which he then undoes by shouting his true one.
Polyphemus's curse, invoking Poseidon, motivates the god's hostility for the rest of the poem.
The Cyclopes lived in Sicily near Mount Etna.

summary: Where Odysseus blinds the man-eating Cyclops Polyphemus and escapes clinging to the belly of a ram — and where he makes his fatal mistake, giving his real name.
myth: Odysseus and twelve men are trapped in the cave of Polyphemus, a one-eyed son of Poseidon, who eats several of them. Odysseus gets him drunk, tells him his name is "Nobody," and blinds his single eye with a sharpened stake while he sleeps. The trick with his name lets them escape when Polyphemus's neighbours ask who hurt him and he answers "Nobody" — but Odysseus cannot resist shouting his real name as they sail off, letting Polyphemus curse him to his father Poseidon by name. That curse drives the rest of the poem's disasters at sea.
historicalBackground: Sicily near Mount Etna, and specifically the rock stacks off Aci Trezza (the "Isole dei Ciclopi"), is the standard traditional setting, partly because ancient authors already associated Sicily with the Cyclopes — but this is later Greek geographical folklore layered onto the poem, not something the Odyssey itself specifies.

name: Aeolia

claims.text: Aeolus gives Odysseus a bag containing the contrary winds.
The crew's decision to open the bag turns the fleet back within sight of home.
Homer describes Aeolia as a floating island, not a fixed real-world location.

summary: Home of Aeolus, keeper of the winds, who gives Odysseus a bag holding every wind but the one he needs.
myth: Aeolus, guardian of the winds by divine appointment, hosts Odysseus for a month and gives him a leather bag containing all the contrary winds, leaving only a favourable west wind to blow him home. Within sight of Ithaca, Odysseus's men — thinking the bag holds treasure he is hiding from them — open it. The released winds blow the fleet straight back to Aeolia, and Aeolus, concluding a man cursed by the gods a second time is not one he should help, refuses to assist again.
historicalBackground: Homer describes Aeolia as a floating island ringed by an unbreakable bronze wall — explicitly not a real place. The Aeolian Islands (Lipari) off northern Sicily borrowed the name in antiquity and are the conventional modern marker, not a location the poem itself supports.

name: Land of the Laestrygonians

claims.text: Laestrygonian giants destroy eleven of the fleet's twelve ships.
Only the ship moored outside the enclosed harbour survives.
Formia, Italy, was the Laestrygonians' harbour.

summary: A harbour of giant cannibals that destroys eleven of Odysseus's twelve ships in a single ambush.
myth: The fleet finds a harbour so enclosed that only Odysseus's own ship anchors outside it. The Laestrygonians, giants, sink the ships trapped inside by hurling boulders and spear the crews "like fish." Only Odysseus's single ship, moored apart, survives — the single worst loss of the entire voyage.
historicalBackground: Formia on the Italian coast (ancient "Lamian Gulf") has carried this association since Roman times — Cicero owned a villa there under that association — but it is a Roman-era literary tradition, not a Homeric specification. The episode's unnaturally enclosed harbour functions as a trap in the story, and matching that geometry to a modern bay cannot turn narrative description into historical coordinates.

name: Aeaea

claims.text: Circe transforms Odysseus's men into pigs and is compelled to restore them.
Circe directs Odysseus to consult the dead before he can find his way home.
Monte Circeo, Italy, is Circe's island of Aeaea.

summary: Island of the sorceress Circe, who turns half the crew into pigs and later becomes Odysseus's guide to the dead.
myth: Circe drugs and transforms Odysseus's scouting party into pigs. Protected by an herb given to him by Hermes, Odysseus resists her magic, forces her to restore his men, and stays with her for a year. She then tells him the one piece of information he needs and could get nowhere else: to reach home he must first sail to the edge of the world and consult the dead prophet Tiresias.
historicalBackground: Monte Circeo, a limestone promontory on the Italian coast, has carried Circe's name since antiquity (it appears on Roman-era maps as such) — an ancient tradition, but still a later identification laid onto a poem that gives Aeaea no real coordinates.
archaeology: The area around Monte Circeo has genuine prehistoric occupation (including a Neanderthal skull found in a nearby cave), which is sometimes cited to lend the identification an air of authenticity — but that occupation predates the Odyssey's setting by tens of thousands of years and has no connection to it.

name: The entrance to the Underworld

claims.text: Odysseus travels to the edge of the world to consult the dead prophet Tiresias.
Tiresias warns Odysseus not to harm the Cattle of the Sun.
Cape Tainaron held a genuine ancient reputation as an entrance to the underworld.
Cape Tainaron is specifically the site the Odyssey describes.

summary: The edge of Ocean, where Odysseus digs a pit of blood to summon the dead and speaks with the prophet Tiresias.
myth: On Circe's instructions, Odysseus sails to the edge of the world, in permanent mist and darkness, and digs a trench filled with the blood of sacrificed animals. The shades of the dead crowd to drink it and speak; among them is the blind prophet Tiresias, who tells Odysseus how to get home and warns him never to touch the Cattle of the Sun. He also meets the ghosts of his mother and of dead companions from Troy, including Achilles and Agamemnon.
historicalBackground: Homer places this at the edge of Ocean, in the land of the Cimmerians who never see the sun — deliberately at the boundary of the known world, not a real destination. Cape Tainaron (Cape Matapan), the southernmost point of mainland Greece, carried a genuine ancient reputation as an entrance to the underworld and is the most common Greek-world candidate, as against Italian sites (Lake Avernus) favoured by the later Roman tradition around Aeneas.
archaeology: A real sanctuary of Poseidon stood at Cape Tainaron in antiquity, and ancient sources including Pausanias describe a cave there popularly believed to be an entrance to Hades — genuine ancient tradition, though not one tied specifically to the Odyssey's own (deliberately vague) geography.

name: Island of the Sirens
region: traditionally the Li Galli islands, Italy

claims.text: The Sirens' song offers knowledge rather than simple physical temptation.
Odysseus survives by being bound to the mast while his crew's ears are sealed.
The Li Galli islands (ancient Sirenusas) are the Sirens' island.

summary: Singers whose voices promise perfect knowledge — and whose listeners never leave alive.
myth: Warned again by Circe, Odysseus plugs his crew's ears with beeswax and has himself bound to the mast so he alone can hear the Sirens' song without being able to steer the ship toward them. The song offers not seduction in the usual sense but omniscience — the Sirens claim to know everything that happened at Troy and everything that happens on earth.
historicalBackground: The small rocky Li Galli islands off the Amalfi coast (also called the Sirenusas — literally "Sirens' islands" in ancient sources) have carried the name since antiquity, making this one of the older traditional identifications, though still not one the Odyssey itself pins down.

name: Scylla and Charybdis

claims.text: Odysseus is forced to choose between the whirlpool Charybdis and the monster Scylla.
Scylla kills exactly six sailors, one per head, as the ship passes.
Ancient geographers already debated whether this episode could be located on a real map at all.
The Strait of Messina is specifically the strait of Scylla and Charybdis.

summary: A strait so narrow that avoiding the whirlpool on one side sails you straight into the six-headed monster on the other.
myth: Odysseus must choose between two evils in a narrow channel: Charybdis, a whirlpool that would swallow the whole ship, and Scylla, a six-headed monster in a cliffside cave who is guaranteed to take exactly six men, one per head, but no more. On Circe's advice he steers toward Scylla, accepting a small certain loss over a total, uncertain one — Scylla seizes six sailors as he passes.
historicalBackground: The Strait of Messina, between Sicily and mainland Italy — genuinely narrow, with real (if much milder than described) currents and whirlpools — has been identified with this episode since at least the time of Thucydides, making it one of the oldest and most persistent traditional identifications in the whole poem, though ancient geographers themselves (notably Strabo's report of Eratosthenes' scepticism) already doubted that Homer's fantastic geography could be pinned to any real strait.

name: Thrinacia

claims.text: The crew, disobeying two separate warnings, kill Helios's cattle out of hunger.
Zeus destroys the ship as punishment, and only Odysseus survives.
Thrinacia's name ("three-cornered") was linked to Sicily's shape already in antiquity.

summary: Sacred cattle that must not be touched — touched anyway, at the cost of every remaining ship and every remaining man but Odysseus.
myth: Twice warned — by Tiresias and by Circe — never to harm the Sun god Helios's sacred cattle, Odysseus's starving, wind-trapped crew kill and eat them while he sleeps. Helios demands justice from Zeus, who wrecks the ship with a thunderbolt the moment it puts back to sea. Every man drowns except Odysseus, who survives by lashing together the wreckage and drifting back past Charybdis alone.
historicalBackground: Ancient tradition already linked Thrinacia — literally "three-cornered island" — to the triangular shape of Sicily (ancient "Trinacria"), making this one of the identifications with real ancient roots rather than purely modern guesswork, though it remains an inference from a place-name pun rather than a specified location.

name: Ogygia

claims.text: Odysseus spends seven years on Ogygia with Calypso before Zeus orders his release.
The poem depicts Odysseus as homesick rather than content despite Calypso's offer of immortality.
Gozo, Malta, is Calypso's island of Ogygia.

summary: Where Odysseus is held, not unwillingly at first, for seven years by the nymph Calypso — the longest stop of the whole voyage.
myth: The sole survivor of the wreck at Thrinacia, Odysseus washes up alone on Ogygia, home of the nymph Calypso, who wants him as an immortal husband and offers him eternal youth to stay. He remains seven years — the poem is candid that desire fades into homesickness, and it opens with him weeping on the shore, wanting only to see the smoke rising from Ithaca again. Zeus finally orders Calypso to release him.
historicalBackground: Homer places Ogygia at the "navel of the sea," far from all other lands — again explicitly remote and not a specified real location. Gozo, Malta, is the most commonly cited modern traditional candidate (a cave there is popularly marketed as "Calypso's Cave"), though the association is a comparatively late and largely tourism-driven one rather than an ancient identification.

name: Scheria

claims.text: Odysseus narrates his own preceding adventures as a first-person account to the Phaeacian court.
The Phaeacians convey Odysseus to Ithaca by ship without demanding anything in return.
Corfu (ancient Corcyra) was identified with Scheria as early as Thucydides.

summary: The last stop before home — where the princess Nausicaa finds Odysseus washed up naked on the beach, and he finally tells his whole story.
myth: Shipwrecked again leaving Ogygia, Odysseus swims ashore exhausted and is found, asleep and naked, by the princess Nausicaa. The seafaring Phaeacians host him lavishly; at a feast he hears a bard sing of the Trojan War and breaks down, at which point he finally reveals his identity and narrates the entire preceding adventure — everything from the Cicones to Ogygia — as a story within the story. The Phaeacians then simply sail him home to Ithaca while he sleeps, asking nothing in return beyond gifts already given.
historicalBackground: Ancient tradition, as early as Thucydides, already identified Scheria with Corfu (Corcyra) — one of the poem's oldest real-world identifications — though the Phaeacians themselves are described as a people apart, uniquely gifted sailors living at the edge of the human world, which is itself a literary device rather than an ethnographic claim about any real islanders.

name: Ithaca

claims.text: Odysseus returns to Ithaca in disguise and kills the suitors occupying his household.
He is recognised by his old nurse via a childhood scar, and by his dying dog Argos.
Modern Ithaki is a poor geographical fit for Homer's description of Ithaca, fuelling alternative identifications.
A Mycenaean-period building on Ithaki can be identified as Odysseus's palace.

summary: Journey's end: twenty years after he left for Troy, Odysseus returns home in disguise to find his palace occupied by suitors besieging his wife.
myth: The Phaeacians leave Odysseus asleep on a beach he does not at first recognise — Athena has disguised both him and the island's landmarks. Disguised as a beggar, he learns that over a hundred suitors have occupied his palace for years, consuming his household while pressuring his wife Penelope to remarry and his son Telemachus to accept it. Recognised only by his old nurse (by a childhood scar) and his dying dog Argos, he strings his own great bow — a feat no suitor can manage — and, with Telemachus, kills every suitor in the hall. Penelope tests him with a final trick about their marriage bed before finally accepting he is really her husband.
historicalBackground: Unlike almost every other stop, Ithaca is not itself in geographical doubt — it is a real, named Greek island. What is genuinely disputed is whether the modern island of Ithaki matches Homer's own description of it (which some ancient and modern readers have found a poor fit, fuelling proposals that Homeric "Ithaca" was instead neighbouring Kefalonia or Lefkada) — a real scholarly debate, unlike the fantastical stops earlier in the voyage.
archaeology: Excavations on Ithaki and neighbouring Kefalonia have found genuine Mycenaean-period remains, including a substantial site at Agios Athanasios on Ithaki sometimes promoted as "Odysseus's palace" — an identification not accepted by most specialists, but resting on real Late Bronze Age archaeology rather than pure invention.
